steps.body: Some rules change formula partway along. A phone plan charges one rate up to 5 GB and another beyond it; that is one function with two formulas, each labelled with the inputs it governs. The labels are what keep it a function: every input is handed to exactly one formula.
Run one branch of the rule.

widget.prompt: This branch applies when x ≥ 0 and its rule is y = 2x + 1. Set the input that produces 9.
widget.successFeedback: x = 4 gives 2(4) + 1 = 9. One input in, one output out — the branch behaves like any other function.
widget.lowFeedback: Output still under 9 — raise the input and watch the doubling do most of the work.
widget.highFeedback: Output past 9 — come back down; 2x + 1 climbs two for every step you take.

predict.prompt: A piecewise rule has two formulas. How many outputs does ONE input receive?

options.label: Two, unless the formulas happen to agree

predict.reveal: The conditions partition the inputs: each x satisfies exactly one of them, so exactly one formula ever applies. If both could fire at the same x, the rule would not be a function at all — which is why the conditions must never overlap.

explanationVariants: x = −3 satisfies x < 0, so the first branch applies and f(−3) = −3 + 5 = 2.
Check the conditions before the formulas: −3 is negative, so the x < 0 rule governs.

widget.prompt: f(x) = x + 5 for x < 0, and f(x) = 2x + 1 for x ≥ 0. What is f(−3)?

options.feedback: Yes — −3 is negative, so the first branch applies: −3 + 5 = 2.
That uses the second branch: 2(−3) + 1 = −5. But −3 does not satisfy x ≥ 0.

options.label: Both 2 and −5
options.feedback: A function returns one output. The conditions decide which formula fires, and only one can.

steps.body: So evaluating happens in two moves, and the order matters: first find which condition the input satisfies, THEN apply that branch's formula. Reaching for the nearest formula and checking the condition afterwards is what produces most piecewise errors.

widget.prompt: With f(x) = x + 5 for x < 0 and f(x) = 2x + 1 for x ≥ 0, what is f(4)?

commonErrors.feedback: Only whole steps here — recompute 2(4) + 1 exactly.
That used the first branch's shape but 4 is not negative, so the x ≥ 0 rule governs: 2(4) + 1.

explanationVariants: Overlapping conditions would give one input two outputs, which no function may do.
The conditions must partition the inputs so each x meets exactly one.

widget.prompt: Why must the conditions of a piecewise rule never overlap?

options.label: Because an input in both would receive two outputs, and functions give one
options.feedback: Exactly — non-overlap is what preserves function-hood.

options.label: Because overlapping conditions are hard to write
options.feedback: Writing them is easy; the problem is that the result stops being a function.

options.label: Because the formulas would have to be identical
options.feedback: They may be anything at all — provided no input satisfies two conditions at once.

explanationVariants: x < 2 and x > 2 leave out x = 2, so exactly one input has no branch.
The conditions miss the single value 2, which makes the rule undefined there.
hints: List the inputs each condition covers and look for one that neither claims.
x < 2 stops just short of 2; x > 2 starts just past it.
The value 2 itself is claimed by neither condition.

widget.prompt: g(x) = 1 for x < 2 and g(x) = 5 for x > 2. How many inputs get NO output at all?

commonErrors.feedback: Look at x = 2 itself: it is neither less than 2 nor greater than 2, so no branch claims it.
Only one value falls through the gap — the boundary x = 2 — not two.

widget.fallbackFeedback: The conditions skip x = 2 exactly, so precisely one input is left undefined.
widget.successFeedback: 1 — the boundary itself. Real definitions close that gap with a ≤ or ≥ on one side.

takeaways: A piecewise function pairs each formula with the inputs it governs.
Evaluate by checking the condition first, then applying that branch.
Conditions must not overlap, or one input would get two outputs.
steps.teaser: Next: draw one — and settle who owns the boundary point.
